item.title: Harnessing laser nuisance achieves record resolution for atomic measurements
item.description: A shoebox-sized color detection device could enable precise measurements at record resolution, according to new research led by Adelaide University. An international team exploited an integrating sphere—a highly reflective hollow cavity that causes light to bounce around inside many times before exiting—to demonstrate a device that can measure the color (wavelength) composition of light with extreme precision at a resolution of just 6 femtometers.

item.title: Repeatable laser measurements reveal 'forbidden' vibrations in single molecules without destroying them
item.description: The possibility of controlling "forbidden" excitations of vibrations in molecules could form the basis of extremely accurate clocks, quantum bits and precise tests of the fundamental laws of physics. Researchers at the University of Basel have now identified and controlled such "forbidden" transitions in single isolated nitrogen molecules without destroying them.

item.title: Laser-driven magnetic state defies equilibrium rules
item.description: Researchers at the Department of Energy's (DOE's) Oak Ridge National Laboratory (ORNL) and their collaborators used lasers and neutrons to observe a long-lived quantum state in a magnetic material, opening a new way to study materials systems driven far from their equilibrium. Manipulation of quantum magnets is important for advancing quantum information science and could reduce loss of transported information, improve memory devices and benefit other quantum technologies.

item.description: Intracavity-doubled green lasers within thousands of laboratories have been quiet for years without anyone knowing why. The answer is the opposite of the obvious one: A nonlinear crystal makes every mode noisier, but the total goes quiet anyway.

item.title: Quantum dot lasers may unlock next era of AI optical interconnects
item.description: A misconception about quantum dot lasers (QDLs) is they’re poised to replace indium phosphide (InP) technology. But InP externally modulated lasers (EMLs) will continue serving optical networking and datacom applications, while QDLs emerge for applications that require power efficiency, thermal resilience, and integration density.
